source.title: Language Models Grow Less Humanlike beyond Phase Transition

page_placements.theme: Interventions on induction heads and the token-index ICL score in small and mid-size models

record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction-head prefix matching during training and relates phase-transition timing to ICL and psychometric predictive power, but it does not reproduce the original loss-bump test or test the proposed circuit composition directly.
record.gate_note: The study measures prefix-matching scores (PS), ICL scores, and their training trajectories. Its main timing comparison is phase transition versus PPP peak, not the claim’s training-loss bump. It also reports head-ablation effects on PPP; those results do not directly measure the claim versions about induction-head mechanism, ICL, or universality and are not rowed here. The text contains no instructions addressed to an AI reviewer.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is reading-time fit (PPP). Along the way it reports its own prefix-matching score (PS) and ICL-score trajectories for 2-layer GPT2 and Pythia-70M/160M/410M. These bear on V2: abrupt PS rise coinciding with an ICL gain, with no loss-bump test. They bear on V4: induction behaviour across two families and sizes. Its syntactic regularization bears on V5: the training setup delays and weakens induction-head formation. It never tests previous-token composition (V1), large-model ICL attribution (V3), few-shot task learning (V6), or sub-steps of induction-head formation (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find PPP peaks coincide with the PS/UAS phase transition across three orders of magnitude (not in MECO). Head ablations do not reliably attribute PPP loss to specific heads. Regularization that delays the transition also delays the PPP peak, so post-transition training dynamics likely drive PPP degradation. No regularizer fully suppressed the transition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the PS induction-head measure and training checkpoints, but focuses on PPP peaks and regularization effects rather than reproducing the original loss-curve/ICL analysis or testing the proposed circuit composition.
record.method_sensitivity: Regularization type and strength affect PS and ICL; SAS suppression delays and weakens induction-head formation, while copying suppression suppresses PS and reduces ICL.

fits_no_version.finding: Penalizing prefix-matching attention in 2-layer GPT2 keeps PS near zero and lowers the ICL score relative to the unregularized model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small transformers, suppressing induction heads during training reduces in-context learning (a causal small-model link).

fits_no_version.finding: In all models, syntactic attention structure emerges shortly before induction heads. Suppressing it delays induction heads, but suppressing induction heads strengthens it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction-head formation is scaffolded by, but does not require, earlier syntactic-attention heads.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study is limited to GPT2 and Pythia models and English reading-time corpora. MECO differs from the other corpora in the reported phase-transition/PPP relationship. The regularization methods only delay or weaken, rather than fully suppress, phase transition. The proposed composition mechanism and the claimed training-loss bump are not directly tested.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports many head-by-head ablation correlations across 5 checkpoints, 5 models, 4 corpora, and two head scores in Section 5, Table 1. They were left out because they measure effects on PPP rather than the claim versions’ induction mechanism, ICL transition, or universality.

untested.parts: Whole version: no previous-token head or composition analysis. PS measures only the induction attention pattern.
The loss bump at the transition. Abruptness is defined by a PS>0.1 threshold, not a slope analysis.
Families beyond GPT2 and Pythia; other architectures and modalities; multiple seeds.
Natural training-data properties. Only regularizers and batch size are varied.
Whole version: no decomposition of induction-head formation.

missing.what: GPT2 2-layer models trained with batch sizes 4, 16 and 64 have different PS transition points. The authors say transition timing depends on the number of updates, not only tokens.
Strong syntactic regularization (UAS near 0) still yields some PS. Induction heads form without syntactic attention.
CopyReg λ=0.01 validation loss rises from ~1B tokens. All regularized models have higher loss than the unregularized one.

record.verdict_notes: Induction-head results are secondary validation of the paper's phase-transition measure. They are qualitative, read from figures, and no uncertainty is given for PS or ICL. V1 was removed from r1–r4 because PS cannot show composition. CopyReg rows were unlinked because the penalty is built against the measured behaviour. The SAS→induction ordering (r15) was not treated as V7, since SAS is a different head type; a reviewer could argue otherwise.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures the copying behavior via PS but does not establish that induction heads form by composing with an earlier previous-token head.
It reports the timing of PS and ICL changes, but does not test whether a bump in training loss occurs at that time. The loss trajectory discussed is validation loss.
Whether induction heads carry most ICL in large transformers.
Other model families, architectures, and modalities beyond the tested GPT2 and Pythia models.
The study varies regularization and reports effects on PS and ICL; it does not systematically vary natural training-data properties.
Whether few-shot task learning mainly uses other heads or mechanisms rather than induction heads.
Whether the observed sequence generalizes beyond the tested models and training setups.
